summary: A fenced island of aspen forest, meadow and lake in the Beaver Hills, 48 kilometres east of Edmonton, and the place that helped save the bison. Plains bison graze north of the Yellowhead Highway and wood bison south of it, alongside elk, moose and some 250 kinds of birds. Paddle among the islands of Astotin Lake, walk the trails, or sit in a bison traffic jam on the parkway.
story: Elk Island lies on the Beaver Hills plateau, called Amiskwaciy in Cree, where the aspen parkland meets the southern boreal forest. Its 194 square kilometres of rolling hills, aspen and spruce forest, bogs, meadows and lakes hold more than 42 kinds of mammals and 250 of birds. It is the only national park in Canada that is completely fenced. Highway 16 splits it in two: a northern block of 134 square kilometres with the plains bison herd, and a southern block of about 60 with the wood bison.

People have lived and hunted here for thousands of years, and hundreds of archaeological sites, mostly campsites and stone-tool workshops, are scattered through the park. The aspen thickets sheltered wintering bison and year-round elk, moose and deer, and the Plains Cree hunted bison on the prairies on horseback and with pounds. The fur trade emptied the hills of beaver by the 1830s, and by 1890 commercial hunting had cut North America's bison from some 30 million to fewer than 1,000. The park lies in Treaty 6 territory and the Métis homeland.

In 1906 five men from the Fort Saskatchewan area persuaded the federal government to protect the last elk of the Beaver Hills. Elk Park, 42 square kilometres around Astotin Lake, was fenced with 24 elk, a few moose and 35 mule deer inside, and Parks Canada calls it the first wildlife refuge in Canada. In 1907 the government bought one of the last big herds of plains bison, the Pablo-Allard herd of Montana, and shipped more than 700 animals north by 1912. Most went on to Buffalo National Park near Wainwright, but about 40 stayed, and today's plains bison descend from them. It became a Dominion Park in 1913.

The park has since sent more than 3,300 plains and wood bison to herds across Canada, the United States and beyond, among them 87 to the Blackfeet Nation in Montana in 2016, 16 to Banff National Park in 2017 and six to Waterton Lakes in 2021. Wood bison from a newly discovered isolated herd arrived in 1965 to preserve their genetics. Beaver were reintroduced in 1942 and trumpeter swans in 1987. Because the fence keeps animals in and large predators are few, Parks Canada actively manages the numbers of bison, elk and moose, and has brought fire back to restore the grasslands.
howItWorks: The park is open around the clock, every day of the year. Entry fees are charged, and youth aged 17 and under get in free. Besides daily admission, Elk Island sells its own annual pass, in person and online, and a machine at the north entrance sells park entry; the Parks Canada Discovery Pass, good at more than 80 Parks Canada places for twelve months, is valid here too. Under the Canada Strong Pass, admission was free for three periods in 2025 and 2026; the last ended on 7 September 2026 and regular fees apply again. Warm summer weekends are very busy, and on long weekends the gates can close temporarily when the park is full.

Camping is allowed only in designated campgrounds, with a permit, and never in a vehicle at a pullout, trailhead or picnic area. Astotin Lake Campground has 75 unserviced reservable sites, 15 of them walk-in tent sites, and five oTENTiks, booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service; from June to September most are taken well in advance. Oster Lake Backcountry Campground has five tent sites, a four-kilometre walk from the Tawayik parking lot; reservations are mandatory and campers register in person at the visitor centre first. Both campgrounds operate from mid-May to Thanksgiving, weather permitting.

Bison are the main hazard and the main attraction. Stay at least 100 metres away on foot, never walk into a herd or between a cow and calf, and when bison are on the road, stay in your vehicle and let them move off; cyclists should pair up with a car to pass. Take extra care in May and June, when cows guard new calves, and in the rut from late July to early September. Black bears, cougars and wolves also live here: keep food and anything scented in your vehicle. Feeding or disturbing wildlife can bring a fine of up to $25,000. Fishing is not allowed, no motors of any kind may be used on the park's lakes, and recreational drones are banned.

sights.name: Astotin Lake
sights.note: The park's centre for picnics, beach, campground and paddling, with many small islands. Canoes, kayaks and paddleboards can be rented; motorboats are not allowed.

sights.name: Living Waters Boardwalk
sights.note: A 400-metre floating boardwalk loop out onto Astotin Lake, with exhibits; 15 to 30 minutes and ideal for small children.

sights.name: Elk Island Pavilion
sights.note: An open-air shelter above the beach built by Depression-era relief workers in the 1930s, the oldest picnic shelter with a chimney in Canada's national parks.

sights.name: Ukrainian Pioneer Home
sights.note: A reconstructed pioneer home with a thatched roof, built in 1951: the first purpose-built structure in Canada to commemorate Ukrainian settlement.

sights.name: Tawayik Lake
sights.note: A lake south of Astotin ringed by aspen and meadow, with a 15.1-kilometre loop trail and views of grazing elk and plains bison.

sights.name: Wood Bison Trail
sights.note: A difficult 15.6-kilometre loop through aspen forest south of Highway 16 — the only trail in the park where you can see wood bison.

sights.name: Oster Lake
sights.note: A waterfowl sanctuary with a five-site backcountry campground on its west shore, a 4-kilometre walk on the Shirley Lake Trail.

sights.name: Wahkotowin Visitor Information Centre
sights.note: The park's visitor centre off Highway 16, opened in 2019, with exhibits made with Indigenous communities, including a bison-hide Star Blanket.

entrances: South entrance off Highway 16 (the Yellowhead), about 48 kilometres from downtown Edmonton — the main gate, by the Wahkotowin Visitor Information Centre
North entrance on Highway 831 south of Lamont, with an automatic pass machine
West entrance on Township Road 544, about 25 minutes east of Fort Saskatchewan
planYourVisit.reservations: Astotin Lake Campground, its group camping area and the oTENTiks are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service, online or on 1-877-737-3783; Oster Lake must be reserved and campers register in person at the visitor centre. On select summer days the Parkbus runs from downtown Edmonton and must be booked. Check before you go with Parks Canada.
permits: Park pass for every visitor, daily or annual
Camping permit for Astotin Lake or Oster Lake
Fire permit for Oster Lake, bought at the visitor centre before you set out
Fishing is not allowed anywhere in the park
camping: Astotin Lake Campground: 75 unserviced sites with showers, kitchen shelter and dump station, 15 walk-in tent sites and five oTENTiks
Astotin Lake Group Camping Area for large groups
Oster Lake Backcountry Campground: five tent sites with pit toilets and fire pits, no drinking water
Quiet hours from 11 pm to 7 am; alcohol is banned year-round at Oster Lake and on long weekends at Astotin Lake
lodging: Hotels and other accommodation in Edmonton, Sherwood Park, Fort Saskatchewan and Lamont
seasonalClosures: Both campgrounds close after the Thanksgiving long weekend and reopen for the May long weekend
Some services in the Astotin Lake recreation area close for the winter — check before you go with Parks Canada

weather: Elk Island is a four-season park. Warm summer weekends are the busiest times, and Parks Canada suggests coming on a weekday or before 11 am on weekends; early mornings bring the best wildlife watching and calmer water on Astotin Lake. Late summer and autumn are the rut for bison, elk, moose and deer. Spring and late autumn are quieter. Winter, from November to April, brings almost a third of the year's visitors for cross-country skiing, snowshoeing, skating and dark skies, with a chance of the northern lights.
directions: The south entrance is about 48 kilometres east of downtown Edmonton on Highway 16, the Yellowhead Highway, which crosses the park for 10 kilometres; the Elk Island Parkway runs 20 kilometres north from there through the park. From the north or east, the north entrance on Highway 831 south of Lamont is often quieter, and from the west there is an entrance on Township Road 544 east of Fort Saskatchewan. Edmonton International Airport is about an hour's drive away. On select summer Thursdays and Saturdays the Parkbus leaves downtown Edmonton in the morning, from MEC and the Royal Alberta Museum, and returns in the afternoon. Check 511 Alberta for road conditions.

chronology.text: After a fire in 1895, the Beaver Hills forest is protected as the Cooking Lake Forest Reserve.
Elk Park is established in July and fenced to protect one of the region's last elk herds — Canada's first wildlife refuge.
Canada buys the Pablo-Allard plains bison herd from Montana; shipments to Elk Island continue until 1912.
Elk Island Park is designated a Dominion Park.
The National Parks Act re-designates it Elk Island National Park.
About 60 square kilometres south of today's Highway 16 is added, now the wood bison area.
Wood bison from a newly found isolated herd are brought to Elk Island to preserve their genetics.
The Beaver Hills Dark Sky Preserve, which includes the park, is designated by the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada.
The Beaver Hills, with Elk Island at its core, become a UNESCO biosphere reserve; 87 plains bison go home to the Blackfeet Nation in Montana.
Sixteen plains bison from Elk Island are moved to the Panther Valley, returning bison to the wild in Banff National Park after more than a century.
The Wahkotowin Visitor Information Centre opens in May.

safety: Bison look placid but can charge without warning. Back away slowly if one snorts, tosses its head, raises its tail or paws the ground, and never ride a bicycle through a herd on the road.
Blacklegged ticks that can carry Lyme disease are present from April to November; check yourself after walking in grass and brush.
Astotin Lake has periodic blue-green algae blooms, which can be toxic, and swimmer's itch. Do not swim, wade or let dogs in the water where a bloom is visible, and rinse off after swimming.

Mobile coverage is patchy. Before an overnight trip to Oster Lake, leave a trip plan with someone and be ready to look after yourself for at least 24 hours; call 911 or Parks Canada Dispatch on 1-877-852-3100.
regulations: Stay at least 100 metres from bison; feeding, enticing or disturbing any wild animal is illegal.
No fishing anywhere in the park, and no gas or electric motors on any lake.
Dogs on a leash and under control at all times; they can provoke bison and moose.
Recreational drones are banned, and collecting plants, antlers, rocks or any natural or historic object is illegal.
Camp only in designated campgrounds; fires only in the fire pits provided.
